newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's aspiring king to fight on for throne.
newsitem.headline: Albania's aspiring king to fight on for throne.

text.p: Albania's would-be king, Leka I, vowed on Monday to continue his fight to restore the monarchy in the chaotic Balkan nation despite a referendum giving a thumbs-down to the throne.

Leka claimed the referendum, held alongside a general election on June 29, was manipulated and refused to accept preliminary results showing a 66 percent vote against restoring the monarchy. Final results are due later this week.
"I don't believe the vote has gone against it," Leka told Reuters during an interview at his heavily guarded villa in central Tirana.
"I can't give up. I have the trust of so many people."

Leka, 58, arrived in Albania in March amid a violent rebellion sparked by the collapse of popular savings funds. This forced the resignation of President Sali Berisha's right-wing Democratic Party government and an early election.

Leka is laying claim to the throne left vacant since his father, King Zog I, fled Albania in 1939, before Mussolini's troops invaded, when he was two days old. Leka was barred from returning during Albania's communist era that ended in 1990.

The bespectacled royal aspirant, who towers above his 3.4 million countrymen at 2.04 metres (six feet eight inches), won Berisha's support to hold a referendum alongside the elections that were intended to end chaos in which over 1,500 died.
The opposition Socialists, reformed heirs to Albania's former communists, scored a landslide victory in the election, ousting the Democrats after five years in power.
Leka accused the Socialists of manipulating the referendum results, but said his fight for the throne was not political.
"The monarchy is above party politics," said chain-smoking Leka, who lives in South Africa with his wife Susan and son Leka.

Before that he lived in Spain for 17 years until he was expelled after the discovery of an arms cache at his home outside Madrid. In 1977 he spent five days in a Thai jail on charges of possessing illegal weapons.
"The only person who has been able to go from one corner of Albania to the other in recent months has been me. The monarchy can bring stability in this country, which has a heavily-armed population."
Despite the dismissal of political links, daily rallies held by Leka and his supporters in Tirana to protest about the referendum have been joined by leading Democrats.

But numbers attending the protests have declined since last Thursday, when one man was shot dead after the rally turned violent. The protest was led by Leka in military fatigues, with a grenade on one hip and a pistol on the other.
On Sunday only about 200 turned up for the rally.
"There is a very strong feeling for the monarchy in Albania," said Leka, who quickly abandoned a military uniform after last Thursday's disaster and returned to his usual wardrobe safari suits.
"If the referendum is deemed to hold, we will have to see what other measures we can take, legal or otherwise.. perhaps the constitutional court.
"I will have to go back to South Africa to sort things out, as my own situation has been neglected for quite a while, but I will be coming back."
Financing his campaign did not appear to be a problem.
"We have a lot of support from Albanians as well as from other friendly sources (overseas)," Leka said, declining to give further details about foreign contributions.
"They want to see the country stabilised. They do not believe a republic can manage that."
